analysis.one_liner: Ends the Federal Reserve's practice of paying banks interest on their reserve deposits.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would stop the Fed from paying banks interest on reserves, went no further than a committee referral and drew no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The Federal Reserve currently pays banks interest on the money they park at the Fed. This bill would strike the legal provision authorizing those payments, effective 180 days after passage. Banks receive tens of billions of dollars a year this way, and the money comes out of what the Fed otherwise sends to the Treasury. The bill was introduced in July 2025 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it has seen no action.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, through the Treasury, which would receive larger payments from the Federal Reserve once it stops paying banks to hold reserves. Ordinary people benefit only indirectly, through a smaller ongoing transfer to the banking system.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes paragraph (12) of Section 19(b) of the Federal Reserve Act, the provision that authorizes the Fed to pay interest on balances, effective 180 days after enactment [S2].

Banks currently earn risk-free interest on reserve deposits; eliminating those payments would redirect that money toward the Treasury, since the Fed sends its leftover earnings to the federal government [S2].
The bill had no cosponsors, indicating no other member of the House had signed on as of its introduction [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks, especially large ones holding the bulk of Federal Reserve reserves, would lose a risk-free income stream. If the Fed loses its main lever for steering short-term interest rates, the cost could show up as less precise control over rates that affect mortgages, car loans, and savings accounts.

drawbacks.text: Paying interest on reserves is the Federal Reserve's primary tool for keeping the federal funds rate on target; stripping it out would force the Fed back to managing a scarce supply of reserves, which historically made short-term rates jump around more, and the 180-day effective date gives the Fed little time to adjust [S2].
Banks could respond by holding fewer reserves at the Fed, which could make the payment system and money markets harder to manage and could complicate the Fed's balance sheet operations [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Ending interest on reserves would stop a genuine, ongoing transfer to the banking system, but the tool it removes is also how the Fed controls interest rates in the modern era. The savings to taxpayers are real, and the monetary-policy cost is manageable only if the Fed successfully retools how it sets rates. A well-designed version would pair the change with a workable replacement framework; this one simply deletes the authority.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it has sat with no hearings, no markup, and no floor vote, and no other member has cosponsored it.

narrative.text: Rep. Warren Davidson introduced the FAIR Act in the House on July 29, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1] [S4].
No further action has been taken; the bill has no cosponsors [S3] [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has been forced to change anything; banks continue collecting interest on reserves while the bill sits untouched in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks keep the payments for now

for.name: Rep. Warren Davidson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strike the Federal Reserve's authority to pay interest on bank reserve balances.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 29, 2025 and has taken no action since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held and no other member signed on, so no partisan split can be measured; the sponsor is a Republican targeting a subsidy to banks.

industries.note: Banks earn risk-free interest on the reserves they hold at the Fed, an income stream this bill would eliminate. The payments come out of earnings the Fed would otherwise remit to the Treasury, so the industry's gain runs against taxpayers' [S2].
Stopping interest payments to banks would leave the Fed with more earnings to remit to the Treasury, a direct fiscal gain for the public [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee action four months after referral, and no scheduled hearing, the bill is almost certain to die quietly when this Congress ends in January 2027.
